source: Ruoss et al. (2024, NeurIPS) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: A transformer trained to predict move values for a board, with no search at play time, reaches grandmaster-level blitz play. This is pattern recognition at scale, the machine version of expert first-workable-option play.
numbers: 270M model: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans (2299 vs bots), puzzle accuracy 95.4%. 136M: 94.5%. 9M: 88.9%. Trained on 10M Lichess games, 15.3B Stockfish-16 action values. Only 14.7% of i.i.d. test boards and 1.33% of puzzle boards were in training.
quote: Despite performing no explicit search, our resulting chess policy solves challenging chess puzzles
limits: Policy cannot plan ahead; it plays greedily on learned values. Elo drops vs bots; occasional tactical errors. Distillation is not perfect. Chess has an exact oracle; open-ended tasks do not.
agent_relevance: A fast recognition pass can carry most of expert skill when training data is huge. A prompt-only scaffold has no such training, so it cannot assume recognition is reliable.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024, NeurIPS) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess (Table 1, search versus no search)
finding: Same paper compares no-search policies with search engines. Adding search still helps; the no-search transformer nearly matches AlphaZero with tree search on puzzles. A general language model (GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct) is far behind.
numbers: Puzzle accuracy (%): ours 88.9 / 94.5 / 95.4 (9M/136M/270M); GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct 66.5; AlphaZero policy-only 56.1, value-only 82.0, 400 MCTS 95.6; Leela policy-only 88.6, value-only 95.9, 400 MCTS 99.6; Stockfish 16 50ms 99.8, 1.5s 100.0. Tournament Elo: ours 2299, AlphaZero MCTS 2470, Leela MCTS 2858.
limits: Mapping of table cells to rows is by column order in the extracted text; check the PDF before quoting a single cell. GPT-3.5 used PGN input, not FEN.
agent_relevance: Search (simulation) adds a measured margin over pure recognition in a rule-exact domain. Recognition plus a check is a sound design; recognition alone is not free.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of Learned Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
finding: Inside Leela Chess Zero's policy network (no explicit search), activations encode future optimal moves and these matter causally. So a pattern-matching network also runs a form of mental simulation.
numbers: A probe predicts the optimal move 2 turns ahead with 92% accuracy (puzzles with a single best line). One attention head (L12H12) moves information backward in time; zeroing a single value has an outsized effect.
limits: Only puzzles Leela solves with a unique line; look-ahead shown for short horizons in certain states, not as a general mechanism.
agent_relevance: Recognition and simulation are not separate in trained networks. In our scaffold they are separate steps by design, which makes them checkable.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025, ICML) Mind Your Step (by Step): CoT can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Test of whether deliberation hurts models where it hurts humans. In implicit statistical learning, CoT cuts accuracy. This is the closest direct machine test of the RPD claim that analysis can degrade intuitive skill.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar): o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o direct 94.0%, a 36.3-point drop (440-problem subset). GPT-4o zero-shot 87.5% vs CoT 64.4% (-23.1, p<0.0001). Llama 3.1 70B -8.8. Eight other models all dropped. Face recognition: all 6 vision-language models worse with CoT (GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2).
limits: 3 of 6 task types showed drops; the other 3 (logical inconsistency, spatial intuition, working-memory preference aggregation) were mixed or helped, because models have priors or long context that humans lack. Models and humans are not parallel in process.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule: keep-first fast mode is safe when the task is perceptual or pattern-like and hard to put in words; force deliberation only where language fits the task.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind Your Step, exceptions-learning task
finding: When labels contain exceptions to a rule, CoT makes models learn the exceptions much more slowly, like humans who theorise instead of memorising cases.
numbers: Averaged over 240 lists, GPT-4o with CoT needed more than 4x the passes of direct prompting; up to 331% more iterations for the worst model. GPT-4o with CoT often never learned all labels within 15 rounds; per-round accuracy stagnated at about 80% (the non-exception share).
limits: Single task adapted from a vehicle classification study (Williams et al. 2013).
agent_relevance: Case memory (retrieval of past episodes) should be allowed to override a stated rule. This matches RPD's use of specific past cases.

source: Sprague et al. (2025, ICLR) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of 100+ papers plus 20 datasets x 14 models: CoT gives large gains only on math and symbolic logic. On commonsense, language understanding and reading comprehension, zero-shot CoT and direct answer are nearly equal. On MMLU the gain is almost all on questions with an equals sign.
numbers: Over 100 papers; own evaluation 20 datasets, 14 models. Direct-answer prompts return the answer within the first 60 characters. Prompt wording changes CoT gain only slightly (tested on Llama 3.1 8B).
limits: Gains reported as averages; some non-symbolic outliers exist. CoT underperforms a symbolic solver on symbolic tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports a router: take the first answer on recognition-type tasks, spend deliberation on symbolic ones. Saves tokens with no accuracy loss.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking (NoThinking)
finding: Skipping the long thinking block (prefilling an empty thinking block) beats full thinking when tokens are held equal, especially at low budgets. Many fast first tries plus a selector can match slow thinking.
numbers: AMC 2023 at 700 tokens: 51.3 NoThinking vs 28.9 Thinking. Below about 3000 tokens NoThinking is better at every k; at about 3500 tokens Thinking is better at pass@1 but NoThinking passes it from k=2. Parallel NoThinking with best-of-N matches Thinking at up to 9x lower latency. Seven datasets (AIME24/25, AMC23, OlympiadBench, LiveCodeBench, MiniF2F, ProofNet).
quote: Notably, the performance of NoThinking becomes more competitive with pass@k as k increases.
limits: One model family (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 32B main; 7B and 14B in appendix, 14B lags at first). LiveCodeBench is an exception where thinking still wins at pass@1. Needs a verifier or confidence signal.
agent_relevance: This is generate-test: cheap first options, then a check. It is the closest published LLM analogue of RPD keep-first mode with a test step.

source: Fang, Ma, Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think
finding: A model trained with RL to choose between a short and a think mode per query. This learns the is-this-situation-typical gate of RPD from reward.
numbers: Cuts use of long-chain thinking by 50% to 90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500 and GSM8K with comparable accuracy (per-benchmark cells not mapped with certainty). Decoupled GRPO prevents the mode collapse seen with vanilla GRPO.
limits: Needs RL training; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B base. Not a prompt-only scaffold.
agent_relevance: The typical-versus-novel gate can be learned. For us it must be hand-written rules or a cheap confidence check.

source: Su et al. (2025, ICLR) Dualformer: Controllable Fast and Slow Thinking by Learning with Randomized Reasoning Traces
finding: One transformer trained on traces with random parts dropped can answer in fast mode (solution only), slow mode (full trace) or auto mode. Fast mode is far better than a model trained only on solutions.
numbers: 30x30 maze: slow mode 97.6% optimal vs Searchformer 93.3% with 45.5% fewer steps; fast mode 80% optimal vs 30% for solution-only; auto mode 96.6% optimal with 59.9% fewer steps.
limits: Synthetic maze tasks plus math fine-tuning; needs training.
agent_relevance: Fast and slow can share one scaffold. The gain comes from letting the system choose between modes.

source: Christakopoulou, Mourad, Mataric (2024) Agents Thinking Fast and Slow: A Talker-Reasoner Architecture
finding: Agent with a fast Talker (System 1) and a slow Reasoner (System 2), shown on a sleep coaching agent. Names the case where the Reasoner must override the Talker.
numbers: No quantitative results reported; qualitative case discussion only.
limits: Design paper; no controlled test. Uses Kahneman's two systems, not Klein's RPD.
agent_relevance: A design pattern with no measured effect. Do not cite it as evidence that the split works.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging Dual Process Theory in Language Agent Framework for Real-time Simultaneous Human-AI Collaboration (DPT-Agent)
finding: Fast rule layer (finite-state machine plus code-as-policy) with a slow LLM layer (theory of mind, asynchronous reflection). Slow thinking alone lowers score through latency; the fast layer acts meanwhile.
numbers: Real-time Overcooked-style game. Human test: 71 university students, 68 valid data points (36 Map 1, 32 Map 2), GPT-4o-mini for all frameworks, 500-step games. DPT-Agent scored highest on both maps; without ToM it still beat ReAct and Reflexion. In Map 2 the version without ToM was preferred.
limits: Simulated kitchen game; one model in the human test; score cells not read one by one. Real-time pressure is the reason for the fast layer.
agent_relevance: Matches RPD in time-pressed command: act on the recognised routine now, reflect in the background. Useful only if our agent has wall-clock limits.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on classic heuristics-and-biases items. It gave the intuitive wrong answer on all Cognitive Reflection Test items and human-like answers on all 12 vignettes, though only 6 were correct. Small changes to vignettes threw it off.
numbers: 12 vignettes: 6 correct, 12 of 12 human-like. CRT1-CRT3: intuitive but incorrect on all 3. Two-step task: 200 simulations.
limits: GPT-3 (2022); later models behave differently. Vignettes are likely in training data, which is why small perturbations matter.
agent_relevance: Old baseline: early models were System-1 only. Current reasoning models need tests on RPD-style cases with perturbations.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024, AIES) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Wargame with 214 national security experts (US-China crisis) versus LLM-simulated teams. Models agree with experts at a high level but are more aggressive, shift with the scenario, and cannot be steered by player traits.
numbers: 214 human experts; first 107 players used for the simulated player data set; models GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. No significant difference on about half of the chosen actions. pacifist vs aggressive sociopath backgrounds gave no significant difference. Simulated team dialogue showed farcical harmony. Counts of significantly different actions as printed: humans 16, GPT-4 10, GPT-4o 9 (two-column extraction, unverified).
limits: Fictional scenario; two moves; models differ from each other.
agent_relevance: A model playing a commander is not a model of an expert commander. Persona prompts did not change behaviour, so do not rely on role prompts to simulate expertise.

source: Rivera et al. (2024, FAccT) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in turn-based wargames. All five models escalated; none de-escalated significantly; sudden unpredictable escalation spikes.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2.0, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base) x 3 scenarios x 10 simulations. GPT-3.5 escalation score rose from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in the neutral scenario.
limits: Simulated nations; authors' own scoring framework; old model versions.
agent_relevance: If a model's first workable option in a conflict is escalatory, a keep-first rule needs a de-escalation check. First options can be biased.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: LLM multi-agent system that plays qualitative wargames end to end (scenario, play, analysis). Two case studies: an AI incident tabletop and a geopolitical crisis.
numbers: No outcome metrics; two demonstration case studies.
limits: Open-source tool and demonstration, not a validation of decision quality.
agent_relevance: A way to run many cheap rehearsals of a plan. Not evidence that outputs match human commanders.

source: Mainali et al. (2025) Classical AI vs. LLMs for Decision-Maker Alignment in Health Insurance Choices
finding: Compares a classical decision maker (case-based reasoning, Monte Carlo, Bayesian diagnosis, naturalistic decision-making) with LLM decision makers (GPT-4 and GPT-5 with weighted self-consistency).
numbers: Overall alignment accuracy: classical 0.892, GPT-5 0.895, GPT-4 0.892. All were best at risk tolerance 0.0; LLMs dropped at the middle target 0.5 while the classical system stayed more stable.
limits: Synthetic health insurance probes; inputs differ (structured numbers vs text); the paper does not test RPD itself. The NDM part comes from Molineaux et al. (2024) military triage work.
agent_relevance: Case-based NDM style agents tie with prompted LLMs on a narrow task. The reasoning model gave no gain over the non-reasoning one here.

source: Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code Review as Decision-Making (CRDM)
finding: Think-aloud study of code review maps reviewer behavior onto Klein's RPD model: an orientation phase builds expectancies, then the analytical phase cycles through RPD. RPD applied to a software task that LLM agents also do.
numbers: 10 participants, 34 code reviews, ethnographic think-aloud plus interviews at one company's software tools department.
limits: Qualitative mapping, small sample, one site; no test of speed or accuracy against alternatives.
agent_relevance: Human reference process for the agent task of reviewing code: build expectancies from context first, then check against them. Relevant to red-team review.

source: Danial, Smith, Veitch, Khan (2019) On the realization of the recognition-primed decision model for artificial agents
finding: Older AI systems that code RPD as cases plus simulation exist (listed as c19 in the E04/01 file). Not re-opened this session.
numbers: Not re-read.
limits: Only cited from an earlier file.
agent_relevance: See the E04 file for detail.

source: Search record: LLM tests of RPD (this session, 2026-11-01)
finding: arXiv listing search for recognition-primed and naturalistic decision making finds few papers. None tests a language model on Klein's fireground paradigm or scores model choices against expert commanders.
numbers: arXiv abstract search for recognition-primed: 1 result (Heander 2025). Naturalistic decision making: 5 results, only Mainali 2025 uses LLMs. WebSearch quota was exhausted; arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned 429.
limits: Absence in titles and abstracts only. Full text of other papers may mention RPD. Confirms the earlier E04 finding (c26).
agent_relevance: The LLM case for RPD stays indirect. A direct test with our own fireground-style cases would be new.

source: Cross-reference: E04/01 evidence_c (SwiftSage, Tree of Thoughts, WebDreamer, RAP, COA-GPT, Reflexion, LATS)
finding: The generate-test and mental-simulation LLM literature is already covered in E04. This file adds work not there: searchless chess, CoT-hurts studies, NoThinking, adaptive thinking, dual-process agents, wargame LLM studies.
numbers: 28 lines listed (c01-c28) to avoid overlap.
limits: Not repeated here.
agent_relevance: Use E04 for simulation methods; use this file for fast-mode evidence and wargame behavior.

source: Synthesis: where a fast first-option mode pays off in machines
finding: Across Sprague, Liu, Ma and Ruoss, first-pass answers match slow reasoning when the task is perceptual, pattern-like or commonsense, or when many cheap tries are verified. They lose on symbolic multi-step problems and when the answer cannot be checked.
numbers: Liu: CoT cost 23.1 to 36.3 points on pattern tasks. Sprague: about no CoT gain on commonsense. Ma: NoThinking 51.3 vs 28.9 at 700 tokens. Ruoss: 95.4% puzzles without search; AlphaZero policy-only 56.1% vs 95.6% with MCTS.
limits: Different models and years; reasoning-model tests mostly on math. Not one controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Rule for the scaffold: keep-first mode only when a cheap test exists or the task is pattern-like; otherwise take the slow path.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Not opened this session. Cited only to anchor the validity conditions for trusting recognition: a regular environment and enough practice with feedback.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Our machine tests are mostly in rule-exact domains (chess, math); the high-validity condition is untested for open military problems.

source: Gap: no LLM study scores first-option satisficing against expert commanders
finding: No source found that measures how often a model's first option is workable, or compares it with expert first options, on RPD-type incident cases.
numbers: None found.
limits: Search budget and API limits; negative result only for the sources reachable.
agent_relevance: Candidate own experiment: give the model fireground-style cases, record its first option, a simulated check and a rival option, and score against expert-labelled outcomes.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT, planning versus execution split
finding: On math and logic tasks, CoT beats direct answering even when the model only has to solve a formal plan, but it still falls short of a symbolic solver. Most of the CoT gain is in carrying out steps, not in choosing the plan.
numbers: Compared direct answer, CoT for plan, CoT for plan and solve, and tool-augmented solver on math and logical datasets (14 models); tool use beat CoT on symbolic execution.
limits: Figures read as text only; exact deltas not copied here.
agent_relevance: Check step: when a test can be run by a tool (code, solver), use the tool as the mental-simulation check rather than prose reasoning.

source: Ma et al. (2025) NoThinking, selection and exceptions
finding: NoThinking's advantage depends on a selector. With a task verifier or simple confidence-based best-of-N it beats Thinking at low token budgets on most benchmarks; with no way to choose among tries the pass@1 result is weaker at high budgets.
numbers: Latency measured as max tokens across N parallel trials. Confidence-based selection beat Thinking under low budgets on most of seven benchmarks. LiveCodeBench: thinking won at pass@1 because disabling thinking did not cut tokens much.
limits: Verifier-based tasks (proofs, code tests) favour the method; open-ended tasks without a verifier are untested.
agent_relevance: Keep-first only pays with a test. Our schema should name the test before allowing the fast option.
